# Classification: Mapping the Terrain {#sec-classification}

## Approach

Before evaluating harmonization potential, every question must be classified into a common vocabulary. Two independent large language models — OpenAI GPT-5-mini and Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 — classified each of the 6,954 analyzable questions by Census topic and subtopic.

Using two models from different vendors serves as a built-in reliability check: where both models agree, confidence is high; where they disagree, the classification is flagged for closer examination.

## Agreement

The two models agreed on topic-level classification for 89.2% of questions (Cohen's κ = 0.839), indicating near-perfect agreement. Subtopic-level agreement was lower at 69.7% (κ = 0.687), reflecting the finer granularity and greater ambiguity of subtopic distinctions.

Both levels exceed standard thresholds for substantial agreement (κ > 0.6), confirming that the classification task is well-defined and that the resulting taxonomy is not an artifact of any single model's tendencies.

## Topic Distribution

<!-- FIGURE: TBD — needs review of available visuals before selecting -->

The classified questions distribute across five broad Census topics:

| Topic | Approx. Count | Share |
|-------|-------------:|------:|
| Economic | ~2,980 | 42.8% |
| Social | ~2,467 | 35.5% |
| Housing | ~967 | 13.9% |
| Demographic | ~369 | 5.3% |
| Government | ~167 | 2.4% |

Economic and Social questions together account for more than three-quarters of all survey content, reflecting the Census Bureau's core mission areas.

## Cost and Efficiency

The complete dual-model classification of all questions cost approximately $15 in API fees and completed in roughly two hours of wall-clock time. A traditional manual classification of this scope would represent weeks of analyst effort.
